lessons.unit: Unit 1: The UK and its connections
lessons.title: Where is the UK? Nations, capitals and the British Isles
objectives: Locate the UK on a world map and describe its position
Name the four nations of the UK and their capital cities
Explain the difference between the UK, Great Britain and the British Isles

keywords.def: the country made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
the island containing England, Scotland and Wales
the group of islands including Great Britain, Ireland and many smaller islands
the city where a country's government sits
where a place is on the Earth's surface

starter: Say Bismillah. How many nations are in the UK? Name them.
What is the capital of each nation?
Which continent is the UK in? Which oceans or seas surround it?

teach.heading: Why study geography?
bullets: Geography is the study of places and the people in them.
It links physical geography and human geography.
Muslims are told to travel and reflect on the Earth (Qur'an 29:20).
teach.note: Welcome pupils to Key Stage 3 geography. Explain physical (natural features and processes) and human (people and what they do) geography. Surah al-Ankabut 29:20 says: 'Say, travel through the land and observe how He began creation.' Cite plainly and invite pupils to say what they would like to explore this year.

teach.heading: Where is the UK?
bullets: The UK is in north-west Europe.
It is about 50° N to 60° N, and close to 0° longitude.
The Atlantic Ocean is to the west, the North Sea to the east.
teach.note: Show a world map and a map of Europe. The UK is an island nation with a population of about 68 million. Point out its position at the western edge of Europe, with the English Channel separating it from France. Ask what advantages an island position might offer (trade, sea routes) and what disadvantages (weather, isolation).

teach.heading: Four nations, four capitals
bullets: England has about 84% of the UK's people.
teach.note: Use a map with colours. England about 57 million, Scotland 5.4 million, Wales 3.1 million, Northern Ireland 1.9 million. Ask pupils why most people live in England. Check that pupils can say all four capitals without prompts.

teach.heading: UK, Great Britain, British Isles
bullets: Great Britain: England, Scotland and Wales only.
UK: Great Britain plus Northern Ireland.
British Isles: also includes the Republic of Ireland.
teach.note: This is a common misconception: pupils use UK, Great Britain and England interchangeably. Use three nested circles on the board. The Republic of Ireland is an independent country, so it is part of the British Isles geographically, but not part of the UK. Some people dislike the term 'British Isles', so mention it is used geographically.

teach.heading: Describing location
bullets: Use continent, country, region and direction.
Example: London is in the south-east of England.
Use compass points and neighbouring places.
teach.note: Model a sentence: 'London is a city in the south-east of England, on the River Thames, in the UK, which is in north-west Europe.' Ask pupils to build the same kind of sentence for another city, such as Manchester, Glasgow or Cardiff.

practice: Label the four nations, their capitals and the surrounding seas on an outline map.
Decide if each statement is true or false: 'England is the same as the UK.' 'Dublin is in the UK.'
independent: Complete a fact file on the UK: location, area, population, nations, capitals.
Write a paragraph describing the location of your own town or city using at least four geographical terms.
Stretch: explain why the terms UK, Great Britain and British Isles are not the same.
exit: Name the capital of Wales and the capital of Scotland.
Is Northern Ireland part of Great Britain? Explain.
lessons.homework: Draw an annotated sketch map of the UK showing the four nations, their capitals and two seas.
lessons.send: Provide an outline map with a word bank. EAL: use colour coding for nations. Stretch: compare the population density of two nations using a table.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: The UK and its connections
lessons.title: The physical landscape of the UK: highlands, lowlands and rivers
objectives: Describe the main upland and lowland areas of the UK
Locate the highest mountain in each nation and the longest rivers
Explain how the physical landscape affects where people live

keywords.def: high land, such as hills and mountains
low, flat or gently rolling land
the shape and height of the land
the wide mouth of a river where it meets the sea
the pointed top of a mountain

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the four nations and their capitals.
What is the difference between the UK and Great Britain?
Name one UK river you know.

teach.heading: Highlands and lowlands
bullets: Upland areas are mainly in the north and west.
Lowland areas are mainly in the south and east.
A line from the Tees to the Exe roughly divides them.
teach.note: Show a relief map of the UK using colours (green for low, brown for high). Ask pupils to describe the pattern. Explain that older, harder rocks form the uplands in the north and west and softer rocks form the lowlands. The Tees–Exe line is a rough guide, not an exact boundary.

teach.heading: Highest points
bullets: Scotland: Ben Nevis, 1,345 m, the UK's highest.
England: Scafell Pike, 978 m. N. Ireland: Slieve Donard, 850 m.
teach.note: Add these to a map. Compare them with Mount Everest at 8,849 m so pupils realise that UK mountains are quite small by world standards, yet weather on them can be dangerous. Ask which of these is in the Lake District (Scafell Pike) as a link to later lessons.

teach.heading: Major rivers
bullets: The Severn is the longest river at about 354 km.
The Thames is about 346 km and flows through London.
Other rivers: Trent, Mersey, Tyne, Clyde.
teach.note: Locate each river on a map. Ask pupils to guess the direction of flow from the source in the uplands to the sea. Many UK cities such as London, Glasgow and Newcastle grew where rivers could be crossed or used for trade. Connect to the Y3 river work if appropriate.

teach.heading: Landscape and people
bullets: Flat lowlands are easier for farming, roads and cities.
Mountains are cold, wet and steep, so fewer people live there.
Uplands are used for sheep farming, forestry and tourism.
teach.note: Link physical geography to human geography. Show a population density map and compare with the relief map. Ask: what do you notice? The densest areas are in lowlands near rivers and coasts. Ask pupils to give two reasons why the Scottish Highlands have few people.

practice: Using an atlas, find the highest point in each nation and record its height.
Describe the pattern of upland and lowland in the UK in two sentences.
independent: Draw a labelled relief map of the UK showing four mountains and four rivers.
Create a table: Physical feature | Name | Location | One fact.
Stretch: explain why more people live in lowlands than in uplands.
exit: What is the UK's highest mountain, and which nation is it in?
Name one UK river and a city on it.
lessons.homework: Research one UK mountain or river and write five facts about it with a photo.
lessons.send: Provide a partly labelled map. EAL: learn 'upland' and 'lowland' with images. Stretch: calculate how many times higher Ben Nevis is than Slieve Donard.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: The UK and its connections
lessons.title: All about London: the UK's capital city
objectives: Locate London on a map and explain why it grew beside the Thames
Describe how London has grown over time
Give key facts about London's people and economy

keywords.def: having a large number of people living in a small area
having people from many different cultures and backgrounds
jobs that provide services, such as banking, tourism and education
one of the 32 local council areas that make up Greater London
visiting a place for leisure or interest

starter: Say Bismillah. Which nation is London in?
Which river flows through London?
What do you already know about London? Write down three things.

teach.heading: Where is London?
bullets: London is in the south-east of England.
It lies on the River Thames, about 80 km from the sea.
About 9 million people live in London.
teach.note: Point to London on a map of the UK. It is the capital of both England and the UK. Ask pupils who live in London to describe the area they live in. If your class is online and spread out, ask them to compare their local area with London.

teach.heading: Why did London grow here?
bullets: The Romans founded Londinium around AD 47.
It was the lowest place to bridge the Thames, near the coast.
River and sea routes made it good for trade.
teach.note: Keep the history light, as the school's earlier lesson found that too much history can overwhelm pupils. Focus on geography: site and situation. Site means the exact spot (a gravel terrace beside the river, firm ground and a crossing point); situation means its position relative to other places (close to Europe by sea).

teach.heading: How London has grown
bullets: Medieval London was a small walled city.
In the Industrial Revolution it grew very fast.
Today Greater London has 32 boroughs plus the City of London.
teach.note: Show maps of London in 1700, 1850 and today if possible. Ask pupils to describe the change in size. London's growth was fuelled by trade, the docks, railways and migration. The Great Fire of 1666 destroyed much of the old city and led to rebuilding in brick and stone.

teach.heading: People and jobs
bullets: More than 300 languages are spoken in London.
Most jobs are in services: finance, tourism, law, media.
teach.note: Explain the tertiary sector. London is a world city: the City of London and Canary Wharf are major financial centres. Many cultures and religions live side by side; mosques, such as the East London Mosque, and the London Central Mosque in Regent's Park are part of the city's landscape. Emphasise respect and understanding for everyone.

teach.heading: Visiting London
bullets: Famous sights: Tower of London, British Museum, London Eye.
Millions of tourists visit every year.
Transport links: Tube, buses, rail, airports.
teach.note: Show images of the landmarks. Tourism is a large part of London's economy but it can also cause crowding. Briefly introduce the idea of benefits and problems. Lead into the independent task by explaining how a tourist brochure uses facts to persuade people to visit.

practice: Fill in a factfile: location, river, population, nickname, three landmarks.
Explain in two sentences why London grew where it did.
independent: Design a tourist brochure or poster for London with at least five facts and a map.
Write a paragraph explaining how London's location helped it grow.
Stretch: compare London's site with that of another river city, such as Glasgow or Newcastle.
exit: State two reasons why London grew by the Thames.
lessons.homework: Finish your tourist brochure and add a section about how visitors can look after London.
lessons.send: Provide a brochure frame with headings and sentence starters. EAL: a picture dictionary for landmarks. Stretch: investigate the difference between 'site' and 'situation' using London as an example.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: The UK and its connections
lessons.title: Where do people live in the UK? Population distribution
objectives: Define population density and distribution
Describe the pattern of population distribution in the UK
Explain why some areas are densely populated and others sparsely populated

keywords.def: how people are spread out across an area
the average number of people living in one square kilometre
having few people living in an area
relating to towns and cities
relating to the countryside

starter: Say Bismillah. Why did London grow beside the Thames?
What does 'densely populated' mean?
Is the Scottish Highlands upland or lowland?

teach.heading: Distribution and density
bullets: Density is the number of people per square kilometre.
teach.note: Work through a quick example: a town with 10,000 people in 50 km² has a density of 200 people per km². Ask pupils to calculate another example. The UK average density is about 280 people per km² but this masks huge differences across the country.

teach.heading: The UK pattern
bullets: The south-east of England is most densely populated.
Big cities: London, Birmingham, Manchester, Glasgow.
The Scottish Highlands have very few people per km².
teach.note: Show a population density map. England's density is about 430 people per km² and Scotland's about 70. Ask pupils to describe the pattern using compass directions and place names. They should notice that dense areas run from the south-east up through the Midlands to the north-west.

teach.heading: Why do people live there?
bullets: Jobs, services, transport and flat land attract people.
Cold, wet, steep land puts people off.
Ports, rivers and coalfields helped some cities grow.
teach.note: Give a table of factors: relief, climate, jobs, transport, history. Ask pupils to apply them to two contrasting places: Greater London and the Scottish Highlands. Look for cause and effect language: 'because', 'which means', 'so'.

teach.heading: Pushing and pulling
bullets: Push factors: reasons to leave a place.
Pull factors: reasons to move to a place.
Today many people move from rural areas to cities.
teach.note: Ask pupils to give an example of a push factor (lack of jobs) and a pull factor (university, work, family). Note that people also move from cities to the countryside for space and lower prices. Link the idea of migration within the UK to the next stages of the unit.

practice: Calculate the population density for two towns using the data table.
Describe the pattern shown on the density map in three sentences.
independent: Write a paragraph: 'Why is the south-east of England densely populated?'
Draw a labelled sketch map showing three densely and three sparsely populated areas.
Stretch: explain how the physical and human factors interact to affect population density.
exit: Give two reasons why the Highlands of Scotland have few people.
lessons.homework: Find the population density of your local council area and compare it with the UK average.
lessons.send: Provide a density calculation scaffold. EAL: give a bilingual glossary of density terms. Stretch: analyse an urban versus rural density graph.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Reading the landscape: OS maps and the Lake District
lessons.title: Ordnance Survey maps: grid references, symbols and scale
objectives: Use four- and six-figure grid references accurately
Identify common OS map symbols
Measure distance using scale and describe direction using compass points

keywords.def: numbers used to give an exact location on a map
the link between distance on the map and distance on the ground
a small picture or sign on a map that stands for a feature
the box that explains what symbols mean
the national mapping agency that makes detailed maps of Great Britain

starter: Say Bismillah. Do you read the easting or northing first in a grid reference?
What does 'along the corridor, up the stairs' remind us?
Name two physical features and two human features you might see on a map.

teach.heading: Why use OS maps?
bullets: OS maps are detailed and accurate.
They help walkers, planners and emergency services.
They show both physical and human features.
teach.note: Show an OS Explorer map extract of the Lake District. Ask pupils what they notice at first glance (colours, lines, symbols). Explain that Explorer maps have a scale of 1:25,000 and are used by walkers; Landranger maps at 1:50,000 are for wider areas.

teach.heading: Four- and six-figure grid references
bullets: Four figures give a square; six figures give a point.
Divide each square into tenths for the third and sixth digits.
teach.note: Common misconceptions from the school's plan: pupils sometimes read the square above and to the right of the numbers instead of to the right of and above the crossing; the reference refers to the bottom-left corner. Use a grid on screen and model two examples: 4-figure 2306, then 6-figure 234067.

teach.heading: Symbols and the key
bullets: Blue: water, such as lakes, rivers and streams.
Green: woodland, parks and nature reserves.
Black: roads, railways and buildings. Brown/orange: contours and paths.
teach.note: Display the OS key with 12 common symbols: church with spire, church with tower, youth hostel, campsite, car park, information centre, viewpoint, picnic site, public footpath, bridleway, railway, post office. Play a quick 'symbol bingo' game.

teach.heading: Scale and distance
bullets: On a 1:25,000 map, 4 cm equals 1 km.
Measure with a ruler or a piece of string.
Use compass points to give direction.
teach.note: Give two worked examples: 6 cm on the map is 1.5 km. Use string to measure a winding path and compare with straight-line distance. Direction: the youth hostel is north-west of the church. Check that pupils use 8-point compass directions.

practice: Give the four-figure and six-figure grid references of the car park shown.
Match 8 OS symbols to their names.
independent: Complete the OS skills worksheet on the Ambleside map extract.
Measure the distance of the path from the car park to the viewpoint and give its direction.
Stretch: plan a 3 km route linking five features and describe it using grid references.
exit: Give the six-figure grid reference for a feature on the map (teacher's choice).
lessons.homework: Draw a key with ten OS symbols and write what each means.
lessons.send: Provide a grid reference support sheet with a clear 'along then up' reminder. EAL: pre-teach symbols with pictures. Stretch: introduce eight-figure grid references.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Reading the landscape: OS maps and the Lake District
lessons.title: Contour lines and relief on OS maps
objectives: Explain what contour lines show
Identify hills, valleys, steep slopes and gentle slopes from contours
Describe the relief of an area using height and slope

keywords.def: a line on a map joining places of the same height above sea level
a number on a map giving the exact height of a point
the height and shape of the land
how steep a slope is
the highest point of a hill or mountain

starter: Say Bismillah. Give a six-figure reference for the church on the map.
What does 1:50,000 mean?
What colour shows water on an OS map?

teach.heading: What are contours?
bullets: Contours join points of equal height.
They are brown or orange lines on OS maps.
teach.note: Use a model of a hill (a lump of clay or sand) sliced into layers or a transparency view. Misconceptions from the school's plan: pupils can find contours messy, and some believe blue contours show negative heights. On OS maps, contours are brown/orange; blue is for water. A contour never splits or crosses another.

teach.heading: Reading steepness
bullets: Close contours mean a steep slope.
Wide-apart contours mean a gentle slope.
Contours usually have 5 m or 10 m between them.
teach.note: Show a hill with a steep side and a gentle side. Ask pupils to say which side is steeper, using the spacing. Link to the idea of 'walking up' a steep slope. Use the phrase 'close together, climbing is tough; far apart, an easy path'.

teach.heading: Shapes in contours
bullets: Rings of contours: a hill or mountain summit.
V-shapes pointing uphill: a river valley.
Flat areas have very few contours.
teach.note: Show examples of a conical hill, a ridge and a valley. Ask pupils to sketch them. The V of the valley points upstream (uphill). A spot height or triangulation pillar marks the top of a summit. Check understanding with an on-screen contour quiz.

teach.heading: Describing relief
bullets: Give heights from spot heights and contours.
Say whether land is high, low, steep or gentle.
Use compass points: 'steep slopes to the north'.
teach.note: Model a description: 'The land rises from 100 m in the south to 650 m in the north. The slopes are steepest near the summit, where contours are close together.' Provide sentence starters for pupils who need support.

practice: Look at a contour diagram and label the steepest slope and the summit.
Draw contour lines for a simple hill in a grid.
independent: Describe the relief of the Helvellyn area using heights and slope in a paragraph.
Draw a cross-section along a line on the map and mark the steepest part.
Stretch: explain why a path between two points might be longer but easier than a direct route.
exit: What colour are contour lines on an OS map?
lessons.homework: Find a local hill or park on an online OS-style map and note the contour pattern.
lessons.send: Provide a partly drawn cross-section. EAL: use 3D models or pictures to teach contours. Stretch: calculate the gradient between two points.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Reading the landscape: OS maps and the Lake District
lessons.title: More about the Lake District: landforms and land uses
objectives: Locate the Lake District and describe its main features
Identify landforms created by glaciers using an OS map
Describe how land is used in the Lake District

keywords.def: a protected area of beautiful countryside where people live and work
a large mass of ice that moves slowly downhill
a long, narrow lake in a glacial valley
the business of visitors coming to a place for leisure
growing and managing trees for timber

starter: Say Bismillah. What do close contour lines show?
Give a four-figure grid reference for a feature on the map.
What is a National Park? Name one you know.

teach.heading: Where is the Lake District?
bullets: It is in Cumbria, in north-west England.
It became a National Park in 1951.
It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2017.
teach.note: Locate it on a map of England. It is about 2,360 km² and has England's highest mountain (Scafell Pike, 978 m), the longest lake (Windermere, about 18 km) and the deepest lake (Wastwater, 79 m). Fun fact: only Bassenthwaite is officially called a 'lake'; the others are 'meres' or 'waters'.

teach.heading: Landforms made by ice
bullets: Glaciers shaped the Lake District over 10,000 years ago.
U-shaped valleys such as Langdale were carved by ice.
Ribbon lakes like Windermere fill glacial valleys.
teach.note: Show photographs of Langdale and Windermere. Explain that glaciers carved valleys and corries (armchair-shaped hollows) with tarns (small lakes) such as Red Tarn on Helvellyn, and sharp ridges called arêtes such as Striding Edge. Use the OS map to spot long narrow blue areas and close contours.

teach.heading: Land uses
bullets: Sheep farming: Herdwick sheep graze on the fells.
Forestry, for example at Grizedale Forest.
Reservoirs such as Thirlmere supply water to Manchester.
teach.note: Ask pupils what OS symbols or colours would show these uses. Explain that quarrying, such as slate at Honister, was also important. Mention that around 40,000 people live in the National Park and many jobs depend on farming and tourism.

teach.heading: Tourism
bullets: Over 15 million visits are made each year.
People walk, climb, sail, cycle and visit villages.
Tourism creates jobs but can cause problems.
teach.note: Brainstorm activities: walking, surfing (wind surfing and paddleboarding on the lakes), boat trips and visiting attractions. Ask which are 'industries' (tourism supports shops, hotels, cafés). Introduce honeypot sites such as Ambleside, Keswick and Windermere.

practice: Using the OS extract, identify two glacial landforms and give their grid references.
List four land uses visible on the map and the evidence for each.
independent: Complete the Lake District worksheet: identify landforms and land uses on the OS extract and note the evidence.
Write a paragraph: 'How is land used in the Lake District?' with named examples.
Stretch: explain why glacial landforms make the Lake District attractive to tourists.
exit: Name one landform created by a glacier.
Give two ways land is used in the Lake District.
lessons.homework: Research one tourist attraction in the Lake District and design a postcard with a caption.
lessons.send: Provide a landform matching sheet and a partly labelled OS extract. EAL: key word cards with pictures. Stretch: analyse how land uses might conflict with each other.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Reading the landscape: OS maps and the Lake District
lessons.title: Protecting the Lake District: conflicts and stewardship
objectives: Describe threats caused by tourism and other land uses
Explain why different groups might disagree about how to use the land
Suggest ways to manage the National Park sustainably

keywords.def: when different groups want different things from the same place
meeting today's needs without harming the future
wearing away of the ground by many walkers
a place that attracts very large numbers of visitors
looking after something that has been entrusted to you

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two glacial landforms in the Lake District.
Give two land uses in the Lake District.
What does 'sustainable' mean?

teach.heading: Threats to the National Park
bullets: Traffic jams and car parking in villages.
Litter, noise and pressure on wildlife.
teach.note: Show photographs of eroded paths and crowded car parks. Ask what happens if thousands of people walk on one path (the ground wears away, the path widens). Charities such as 'Fix the Fells' repair the paths.

teach.heading: Different people, different views
bullets: Tourists want to walk and relax.
Residents want homes they can afford and quiet streets.
teach.note: Set up four groups: farmers, tourists, residents and conservationists/National Park Authority. Highlight second homes and holiday lets, which raise house prices for locals. Ask each group to write one sentence starting 'I want...'. Look for the conflict between groups.

teach.heading: Managing the park sustainably
bullets: Repair paths and build stone steps.
Educate visitors with the Countryside Code.
teach.note: Match each problem with a solution. Ask pupils which solution is the most effective and which is the cheapest. Discuss that stricter rules might protect nature but reduce visitors and income. Encourage balanced thinking and reasons.

teach.heading: Khalifah: caring for the Earth
bullets: Muslims believe humans are khalifah, stewards, on Earth (Qur'an 2:30).
Allah does not like waste or harm (Qur'an 7:31).
We leave places as we found them.
teach.note: Link to the Islamic ethos. Surah al-Baqarah 2:30 mentions that Allah placed a khalifah on the earth. Surah al-A'raf 7:31 says: 'eat and drink, but do not be excessive'. Ask: how can a visitor act as a good steward in a beautiful place? (Take litter home, keep to paths, respect farmers and animals.)

practice: Match each problem with a solution and say who would benefit.
Group role-play: farmers, tourists, residents and park rangers discuss a proposal for a new car park.
independent: Write a letter to the National Park Authority explaining the best way to protect the Lake District.
Complete the table: Problem | Who is affected | Solution | Advantage | Disadvantage.
Stretch: evaluate whether tourism does more good than harm to the Lake District.
exit: Give one problem caused by tourism and one solution.
lessons.homework: Create a 'Visitor Code' poster with five rules for protecting a National Park.
lessons.send: Provide role cards with sentence starters. EAL: pre-teach conflict vocabulary with visuals. Stretch: use evidence to justify a decision and anticipate the other side's response.

lessons.title: Your place 20,000 years ago: glaciers, what and where?
lessons.bigQuestion: What would your home town have looked like 20,000 years ago?
objectives: To understand what glaciers are and where ice covered the land in the past and today
successCriteria: All: say what a glacier is
Most: describe how far ice spread over Britain 20,000 years ago
Some: explain how a glacier forms and moves
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: states of matter and density of ice
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: awe at how the land was shaped over time

keywords.def: a large, slow-moving mass of ice on land
a long, cold period when ice covers much more land
a huge glacier covering a large area of land
a glacier that flows down a valley
the build-up of snow and ice

hook.text: Was your home under ice 20,000 years ago? How could you find out?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'He sends down from the sky, from mountains of cloud within it, hail' (an-Nur 24:43). Ice and snow are part of Allah's creation, and the landscapes we live in today were shaped by them long ago.

starter.q: Which country has the UK's highest mountain?
A contour line joins places of the same:
Ice is water in which state?
Name a large ice sheet today.

teach.heading: What is a glacier?
bullets: Snow builds up year after year
teach.note: Gravity makes the ice move, usually a few centimetres to metres a day.

teach.heading: Britain 20,000 years ago
bullets: Ice covered most of Scotland, Wales and northern England
teach.note: Britain was joined to mainland Europe by land, because so much water was locked in ice.

teach.heading: Glaciers today
bullets: About 10% of land is covered by ice
teach.note: About 10% today; at the peak of the last ice age, much more.

teach.heading: Two kinds of glacier
bullets: Ice sheet: covers a huge area
teach.note: Ask: which kind covered Scotland 20,000 years ago? An ice sheet.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: 20,000 years ago, ice covered:
options: Most of Scotland, Wales and northern England
check.why: Southern England was beyond the ice, though very cold.

practice.q: Describe how a glacier forms.
practice.a: Snow builds up, is squashed into firn and then ice, which flows downhill under gravity
practice.model:
Start: snow builds up each winter.
Next: the weight squashes it into ice.
Then: gravity makes it flow downhill.
So a glacier forms.

practice.q: About what fraction of land is covered by ice today?
practice.a: About 10% (one tenth)

practice.q: Why was sea level lower 20,000 years ago?
practice.a: So much water was locked up in ice on land

independent.q: Core: On a map of the British Isles, shade the ice cover 20,000 years ago and mark your home. Write two sentences on what your area was like.
independent.a: Ice over most of Scotland, Wales, northern England and Ireland; south of that, cold tundra; sentences match the pupil's location
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: shade from northern Scotland down to roughly the Bristol Channel and the Midlands, then mark London outside the ice: 'London was not under ice but was frozen tundra.'

independent.q: Extend: Compare the size of glaciers 20,000 years ago with today.

teach.note: Plucking leaves jagged rock surfaces.

teach.note: This happens above the ice and provides rocks for abrasion.

practice.model:

Step 2: the glacier keeps moving.
Step 3: it pulls the rock out.

exit.a: Snow becomes heavy moving ice that plucks rock, scrapes it by abrasion and is helped by freeze-thaw weathering

practice.model:
I find the highest bar: April, about 200 mm.
I find the lowest: July, about 20 mm.
I spot the pattern: two wet peaks, March to May and October to December.
So: Nairobi has two rainy seasons, wettest in April and driest in July.

lessons.title: Kenya's people and how Kenya earns a living: the flower trade

successCriteria: All: describe Kenya's population and the growth of Nairobi
Most: classify jobs into sectors
Some: weigh the benefits and problems of flower farming
lessons.smsc: Moral: fair pay and care for the environment in what we buy

keywords.def: people moving from the countryside to towns and cities
work that is not officially registered or taxed
goods sold to another country
a crop grown to sell, not to eat
jobs that take raw materials from the land or sea

hook.text: Why might a young person leave a farm to look for work in a big city?

starter.q: Nairobi is about how high above sea level?

teach.heading: Kenya's people
teach.note: Most Kenyans still live in rural areas, but towns are growing fast.

teach.heading: Nairobi grows
teach.note: People come for jobs, schools and services. Many work in the informal economy, called jua kali ('hot sun').

teach.heading: How Kenyans earn a living
teach.note: M-Pesa, mobile phone money, was launched in Kenya in 2007.

teach.heading: The flower trade
bullets: Kenya is a leading exporter of cut roses
teach.note: Flowers bring jobs and foreign money, but raise questions about water and workers' pay.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Packing roses in a cold store is which sector?
check.why: Processing and packing products is secondary; growing them is primary.

practice.q: Explain one benefit of the flower trade to Kenya. (2 marks)
practice.a: It creates jobs (1), many for women in rural areas, giving families a steady income (1)
practice.model:
Point: it creates jobs.
Develop: thousands work on farms near Lake Naivasha, many of them women, so families gain a regular wage.

practice.q: What is rural-urban migration?
practice.a: People moving from the countryside to towns and cities

practice.q: Is a safari guide primary, secondary or tertiary?
practice.a: Tertiary

independent.q: Core: In the portal response box, answer: 'Is the flower trade good for Kenya?' (6 marks). Give two benefits, two problems and a judgement.
independent.a: Benefits: jobs, income, infrastructure; problems: water use at Naivasha, pesticides, pay; a supported judgement
independent.model: Teacher models the first benefit paragraph using Point, Evidence, Explain.

independent.q: Extend: Why might Kenya want to sell more processed goods rather than raw crops?
independent.a: Processed goods sell for more money and create more jobs at home

independent.q: Stretch: Is it fairer to buy Kenyan roses or UK roses grown in heated greenhouses? Consider carbon.
independent.a: Kenyan roses are flown in, but UK winter roses need heated greenhouses, which can use more energy; a reasoned judgement

exit.q: A cash crop is grown to:
exit.a: Sell

exit.q: Kenya's flower farms are mainly near:
exit.a: Lake Naivasha

exit.q: Big question: who grew your rose, and where?
exit.a: Probably workers on a flower farm near Lake Naivasha, Kenya, for export to Europe

say what is there or what the pattern is
give reasons why or how
numbers that locate a square or point on a map
a decision backed by evidence

check.q: To describe a graph you should:
check.why: Describe = pattern plus data; explain = reasons.

practice.q: What do you do if stuck?
practice.a: Move on and come back

independent.q: Q1 (3): Name a landform of glacial erosion, a landform of glacial deposition, and the process where ice breaks rock by freezing and thawing.
independent.a: For example: corrie or arete (1); moraine or drumlin (1); freeze-thaw weathering (1)
independent.model: Teacher reads Q1 aloud and shows how 3 marks means three answers.

independent.q: Q2 (4): Explain how a meander becomes an ox-bow lake.
independent.a: Erosion on the outer bends (1) narrows the neck (1); a flood breaks through the neck (1); deposition seals the old loop (1)

independent.q: Q3 (2): Give two causes of river flooding.
independent.a: Heavy or long rainfall; impermeable surfaces, deforestation or saturated ground (any two)

independent.q: Q4 (3): Describe the location of Kenya.
independent.a: East Africa (1); on the Equator (1); borders such as Tanzania, Uganda, Ethiopia, or the Indian Ocean coast (1)

independent.q: Q5 (4): Explain why population density in Africa is uneven.
independent.a: Dense where there is water, fertile soil and cities, e.g. the Nile valley (2); sparse in deserts like the Sahara (2)

independent.q: Q6 (4): Using the climate graph (Nairobi), describe two features of the climate.
independent.a: Two rainy seasons with figures (2); mild temperatures all year, about 17 to 20 °C (2)

independent.a: Level answer: jobs, income and infrastructure against water use, pesticides and pay, with a supported judgement

Some: write a balanced judgement

keywords.def: improving people's lives: health, wealth and education
a measure used to compare development
how long a person can expect to live on average
the percentage of adults who can read and write
information on what went well and what to improve

hook.text: What would you measure to decide if a country's people are better off than 20 years ago?
